title: Load synthesis variance attribution cheat sheet
content:
Purpose:
This is a working cheat-sheet for rapidly diagnosing throughput variance in our load synthesis runs. Intended for engineers running repeatability experiments and for on-call/bench triage. Not a formal protocol (see other playbooks) — think fast heuristics + reproducible mini-experiments.

High-level goals (what I want to know within 30–90 minutes):
- Is the variance source internal (runtime scheduling, kv cache behavior, batching nondeterminism) or external (node thermal throttling, noisy co-tenants, network jitter)?
- Which signal(s) correlate strongest with drops (GPU utilization, cpu steal, context-switches, NVLink errors, p99 latency)?
- Can I design a 15–20 minute isolating experiment that changes one factor at a time?

Quick triage checklist (fast, actionable):
1) Re-run with fixed seeds + identical request payloads for 5–10 minutes. If variance persists, external/system-level causes likely.
2) Switch from Poisson arrivals to deterministic spacing (fixed inter-arrival) and compare. Poisson adds arrival noise; deterministic shows server-side noise more clearly.
3) Inspect host-level metrics: core throttling, dmesg for OOM/thermal messages, nvidia-smi log for ECC or clock changes.
4) Confirm client-side pacing isn't contributing: check client clock skew, container cpu limits, or thread scheduling on the load generator.
5) Toggle KV/Prefix cache hit ratio (simulate cold vs hot): if cold runs stable but hot runs noisy, suspect cache eviction or KV cache synchronization.

Design patterns for isolating variables:
- Micro-anchoring: keep a tiny canonical workload (e.g., prompt length 32 tokens, deterministic output sampling) and run repeated short cycles. Use this as a baseline anchor across all experiments.
- Single-factor sweeps: change only request concurrency or request size; keep everything else identical. Use at least 3× repeats per condition.
- Component toggles: run with and without batching enabled, quantized model binary, or GPU persistence mode to see step changes.

Load synth recipes (copy/paste friendly examples):
1) Deterministic step ramp (good for comparing priming effects):
- 30s idle
- 60s at 10 qps
- 120s at 50 qps
- 120s at target qps (e.g., 200)
- 60s cooldown
Rationale: short anchors and a plateau let you observe stabilization times and oscillation.

2) Poisson-smeared steady state (realistic traffic):
- Warmup 3 minutes at 20% target qps
- Sustained 20 minutes at target qps, arrivals drawn Poisson(lambda)
- Compare sample windows: first 2m vs last 2m to detect drift.

3) Microburst probe (find burst fragility):
- Sustained baseline 50% target qps
- Inject 5s microbursts at 5× baseline every 90s for 15 minutes
- Observe tail latency and retry/backpressure signals

Repeatability knobs (must set explicitly in every run):
- RNG seed for any synthetic content or sampling (client and any stochastic server components)
- Exact prompt text and truncation/concatenation policy
- Client machine CPU pinning and real-time priority (or lack thereof)
- Network path (same subnet, same NIC drivers), ideally isolated VPC subnet
- Duration of sample windows (use 95% trimmed mean over >=10k tokens where possible)

Observability checklist (metrics/time-series to gather):
- GPU: utilization, mem utilization, average/peak active SMs, clock changes, power caps, GPU temperature, nvlink errors
- Host: CPU steal, loadavg, kernel scheduler latencies, cgroup throttling, irq/softirq rates
- Process: RSS, page faults, GC pauses (if runtime has GC), thread counts, fds usage
- Server runtime: batching size distribution, average tokens/sec, kv cache hit rate, eviction rate, queue lengths per worker
- Network: p95/p99 client-server RTT, retransmits, NIC errors
- Application-level: model load times, session affinity changes, fallback-to-cpu events

Attribution heuristics (how to interpret signals):
- Variance correlated with GPU temperature / clock changes -> thermal throttling or power management. Check dmesg + DCGM logs.
- Variance correlated with CPU steal or high system time -> noisy co-tenant or kernel activity. Run isolating experiment on dedicated host.
- Spikes in softirq/irq -> NIC or driver interrupts; test with kernel driver toggles and NIC IRQ affinity.
- Queue-length oscillation + increased batching variance -> internal throttling/backpressure; inspect per-worker queue histograms.
- Sudden increase in KV evictions immediately before throughput drop -> cache pressure/regeneration cost. Consider increasing KV cache size or pinning critical keys.

Statistical sanity checks (quick):
- Compare medians and 95th; if means differ but medians don't, noise is in the tails.
- Use bootstrapped confidence intervals across repeats. If CI overlap across conditions, treat differences as inconclusive.
- Use autocorrelation on the throughput time series; persistent autocorrelation suggests a slow state change rather than white noise.

Mini-experiment templates (15-minute runs):
Template A — suspect client jitter:
- 2 min deterministic baseline (fixed spacing) at 20%
- 8 min target qps deterministic
- 2 min target qps Poisson
- 3× quick repeats, capture client CPU, clock skew, and threads
Interpretation: if deterministic->Poisson step changes throughput significantly, client pacing may be introducing noise.

Template B — suspect runtime batching instability:
- 10 min baseline at 60% qps with batching ON
- Toggle to batching OFF for 5 min, revert back for 5 min
- Record per-batch size histogram and per-worker queue lengths
If batch-on segments show markedly higher variance, dig into batching heuristics and threshold timers.

Practical gotchas (notes to self):
- Don’t trust a single long run — thermal and cloud maintenance events can bias long-duration runs. Prefer multiple short repeats with identical anchors.
- Cloud autoscaling/metadata agents sometimes trigger kernel tasks; use dedicated nodes for bench runs when possible.
- GPU persistence mode reduces scheduling variance on some drivers — flip it if you see unexpected clock changes.
- Mixed tenancy on NIC (shared infra) can add micro-jitter even when host metrics look fine.

Automation and artifacts to capture (what to upload with a ticket):
- Loadgen config (exact command line), seed, and client machine spec
- Raw time series (1s resolution) for throughput, p50/p95/p99 latencies, batch sizes, GPU counters, host metrics
- Short screen recording or flamegraph if interactive debugging used
- Minimal reproducer script that runs a single canonical workload for 3× repeats and captures outputs

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can we add a small deterministic tracer token in requests to align events across distributed traces? Would help correlate server events with exact request IDs. (Mei to prototype)
- Is there a low-overhead host-level probe we can run to detect thermal throttling earlier? Might be kernel event subscription. (Rafael exploring)

Appendix — example loadgen snippet (golang-like flags):
--target-qps=200 \
--arrival-mode=deterministic \
--seed=14327 \
--duration=1200s \
--request-template=prompts/anchor-32.jsonl \
--client-cpu-cpus=4 \
--sample-window=10s

Final note: keep a short experiment log appended to the ticket. Even one-line notes about cloud host IDs + GPU serial numbers saved me many hours. If a run looks flaky, always re-run on a freshly provisioned dedicated host before escalating.

-- Aisha (bench scratchpad, draft)
